name: Consumer Rights Directive
evidence_rating: thin: Commission evaluations and national assessments only; no causal study of the CRD's effect on cross-border trade, prices or returns
summary: The Consumer Rights Directive harmonised pre-contract information and the 14-day right to withdraw from online and doorstep sales from 2014. Its promised gain - cheaper cross-border selling - was never measured: the Commission's 2017 review found too little data, and the UK's forecast GBP 2.6 billion benefit was not checked after the fact. Reviews show compliance costs are modest but withdrawal rights remain the top cross-border complaint, and the 2024 review flagged subscription traps and simplification needs.

indicators.objective: The 2008 CRD proposal contains no legislative financial statement indicators; Article 30 required a Commission report by December 2016, delivered as the 2017 evaluation

indicators.indicator: Lower compliance costs for cross-border traders by replacing minimum with (largely) full harmonisation
indicators.target_or_baseline: Baseline: 60% of traders saw extra costs of complying with different national consumer laws as an important obstacle to cross-border B2C trade (Eurobarometer 2008)
indicators.evidence: Not measured. The 2017 evaluation found too little data for definitive conclusions on business costs. The UK ex-ante assessment put the harmonisation benefit at about GBP 358m a year for UK business; the UK's 2019 statutory review did not quantify it. Eurostat: 19.1% of EU individuals bought online from sellers in other EU countries (3 months, 2023), not attributable to the CRD.
indicators.sources: SEC(2008) 2544/2545; SWD(2017) 169/170; BIS 2013 IA; UK statutory report 2019; Eurostat isoc_ec_ibos

indicators.indicator: Effective pre-contractual information and 14-day withdrawal right in distance and off-premises sales
indicators.evidence: Partially measured in the 2017 evaluation: right of withdrawal the most frequent cross-border complaint topic (79% of European Consumer Centres say consumers complain often); in mystery shopping 25% of online shops selling goods gave no withdrawal-form information; only 13% of traders aware of the new digital-content rules. 2024 Digital Fairness Fitness Check flags information duties and withdrawal right for simplification.

2024 Fitness Check: costs of UCPD, CRD and UCTD together about EUR 511-737m a year; only 10-18% of traders report high costs. In the 2017 CRD survey a majority of traders said information requirements raised costs, and 44% cited reimbursement rules tied to withdrawal.

literature.citation: European Commission (2008), Impact assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on consumer rights (summary SEC(2008) 2545), SEC(2008) 2544
literature.title: Impact assessment accompanying the proposal for a Directive on consumer rights (summary SEC(2008) 2545)
literature.outcomes: fragmentation costs; cross-border trade; consumer confidence
literature.headline: Minimum-harmonisation clauses fragment national rules; 60% of traders see compliance with different national laws as an important obstacle; full harmonisation expected to boost cross-border sales and confidence
literature.summary_plain: The Commission argued that one set of consumer-contract rules would make it cheaper for shops to sell across borders and give shoppers more confidence.

literature.citation: UK Department for Business, Innovation and Skills (2013), Implementation of the EU Consumer Rights Directive (2011/83/EU): Impact Assessment - Final, BIS/13/1367 (IA BIS0396)
literature.authors: UK Department for Business, Innovation and Skills
literature.title: Implementation of the EU Consumer Rights Directive (2011/83/EU): Impact Assessment - Final
literature.headline: Net present value GBP 2.57bn over 10 years (range 2.07-3.08bn); benefits dominated by an assumed GBP 358m a year from harmonisation; main ongoing cost GBP 56m a year from extended cancellation rights in distance sales
literature.summary_plain: The UK government expected the directive to bring a net benefit of about GBP 2.6 billion over ten years, almost all from easier cross-border selling - an assumption, not a measurement.
literature.quality: forecast; benefit rests on harmonisation assumption

literature.citation: European Commission (2017), Evaluation of the Consumer Rights Directive (executive summary SWD(2017) 170) and Report COM(2017) 259, SWD(2017) 169
literature.title: Evaluation of the Consumer Rights Directive (executive summary SWD(2017) 170) and Report COM(2017) 259
literature.method: review (CRD study: surveys, mystery shopping, consultation)
literature.headline: Directive in line with objectives of enhancing protection and reducing fragmentation, but evaluated early; too little data to conclude on business costs; withdrawal right the most common cross-border complaint; 25% of online shops tested lacked withdrawal information; recommends extending scope to 'free' digital services
literature.summary_plain: The Commission's 2017 review found the directive had helped, but it was too early and data were too thin to measure costs or benefits.

literature.citation: UK Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy (2019), Statutory Report on the Implementation of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013, BEIS statutory review (July 2019)
literature.authors: UK Department for Business, Energy and Industrial Strategy
literature.title: Statutory Report on the Implementation of the Consumer Contracts (Information, Cancellation and Additional Charges) Regulations 2013
literature.headline: Respondents generally felt the Regulations still meet their objectives; information and cancellation rules give consumers reassurance to engage; no quantification of the costs and benefits forecast in 2013
literature.summary_plain: Five years on, the UK review found the rules broadly working but did not check whether the forecast GBP 2.6 billion benefit had materialised.

literature.citation: Borges & Irlenbusch (2007), Fairness Crowded Out by Law: An Experimental Study on Withdrawal Rights, Journal of Institutional and Theoretical Economics 163(1): 84-101
literature.title: Fairness Crowded Out by Law: An Experimental Study on Withdrawal Rights
literature.venue: Journal of Institutional and Theoretical Economics 163(1): 84-101
literature.method: causal: laboratory experiment (voluntary vs mandatory withdrawal right)
literature.headline: After Germany legislated a withdrawal right, returns rose sharply though most sellers already offered returns; in the lab, voluntarily offered return rights are reciprocated with less exploitation than legally mandated ones; small return costs barely change behaviour
literature.summary_plain: A lab experiment suggests that when the law, rather than the seller, grants a right to return goods, buyers use it more aggressively - relevant to the cost of the CRD's 14-day withdrawal right.
literature.quality: lab experiment; external validity limited; predates CRD

literature.citation: European Commission (2024), Fitness Check of EU consumer law on digital fairness (executive summary SWD(2024) 231), SWD(2024) 230
literature.title: Fitness Check of EU consumer law on digital fairness (executive summary SWD(2024) 231)
literature.headline: Covers CRD with UCPD and UCTD: effectiveness 'limited'; consumer detriment online at least EUR 7.9bn a year; compliance costs about EUR 511-737m a year; problems with cancelling and renewing digital subscriptions; information duties and the right of withdrawal identified as areas for simplification
literature.summary_plain: The 2024 review found the CRD still relevant and not costly, but weak against subscription traps and other online problems, and suggested simplifying its information and withdrawal rules.
